hints: Focus on the two separate ideas being tested here, the relative mass scale based on carbon-12 and what causes deflection in an electric field.
Remember that both protons and neutrons each weigh about 1 unit on the $^{12}\text{C} = 12$ scale, while electrons are almost 0.
Consider the charge on a neutron and link that to whether an electric field can push it off course.
walkthrough:
**Recall the relative mass of a neutron**

Think of the carbon-12 scale where one atom of $^{12}\text{C}$ is exactly 12 units. A proton and a neutron each have a mass of about 1 unit on this scale.

$$\text{relative mass of neutron} \approx 1$$

**Recall the charge and deflection rule**

Electric fields only deflect charged particles. Protons ($+1$) bend toward the negative plate and electrons ($-1$) bend toward the positive plate.

$$\text{deflection needs charge, no charge means no deflection}$$

**Apply to neutrons**

A neutron is written as $^{1}_{0}\text{n}$. It has mass 1 but charge 0, so it is neutral. A beam of neutrons therefore passes straight through with no deflection.

options.A: Incorrect on both columns. Mass 0 is the relative mass of an electron, not a neutron. A deflected result would also need a charge, but neutrons are neutral.
options.B: Half right, half wrong. Mass 1 is correct for a neutron, but deflected is wrong. This is the proton trap, protons also have mass 1 but they have +1 charge so they deflect, neutrons do not.
options.C: Half right, half wrong. Not deflected is correct because neutrons are neutral, but mass 0 is wrong. This mixes up no charge with no mass, neutrons have almost the same mass as protons.
options.D: Correct on both columns. A neutron has relative mass 1 and relative charge 0, so a beam of neutrons has mass but experiences no force in an electric field and is not deflected.
